explanations.explanation: Verse 1 says it plainly: Jaazaniah son of Azzur and Pelatiah son of Benaiah "were leaders of the people." Out of twenty-five men at that gate, these are the two the text names. That's all it tells us about them, and I won't add more. Leaders are the ones folks listen to, so what the LORD says about them next carries real weight.

I get the guess, friend, since they're standing right at a gate. But standing at a gate doesn't make you a gatekeeper. I stand next to my ovens all day and nobody calls me an oven. The text says these two were leaders of the people.

No instruments and no songs show up anywhere in this scene. The only thing verse 1 says about Jaazaniah and Pelatiah is that they were leaders of the people. It's a quiet gate, and what comes out of it is not a tune.

The LORD says, "…these are the men who plot evil and give wicked counsel in this city." Plotting is planning ahead, and here the plan is evil. God tells Ezekiel, the prophet in this vision, exactly what is going on at that gate. Nothing is hidden from Him.

Counsel just means advice, and these men are leaders, so people listen. The LORD calls their advice wicked. That's the word in verse 2: they "give wicked counsel in this city." Advice from the wrong people gets expensive fast.
That one flips the whole sentence around. If these men hated evil, there would be no trouble at the gate. Verse 2 says they "plot evil," so they're planning it, not pushing it away.
Wise counsel is exactly what you'd hope for from leaders, friend. But verse 2 doesn't call their counsel wise. The LORD says they "give wicked counsel in this city."
Honest advice would be a nice thing to hear from a leader. That's not the word the LORD uses, though. Verse 2 says these men give "wicked counsel in this city," and that's the label God puts on it.

I can see how you got there, but the LORD does the opposite. In verse 4 He says, "Therefore prophesy against them; prophesy, O son of man!" He says it twice, so Ezekiel can't miss it. These men don't get left alone. They get a message from God.
Right, and the LORD says it twice. Verse 4 says, "Therefore prophesy against them; prophesy, O son of man!" Ezekiel isn't told to keep quiet. He's told to speak, and he does.

That's what God says in verse 5: "…I know the thoughts that arise in your minds." Not just the words said at the gate, but the thoughts underneath them. I can walk into my kitchen and forget why I came in. God never loses track of a single thought.
The text says the opposite. In verse 5 God tells the house of Israel, "…I know the thoughts that arise in your minds." Nothing in anyone's head is out of His sight. Even the quiet thoughts count.

explanations.answer: The slain laid within the city
explanations.explanation: That's it. Verse 7 says, "The slain you have laid within this city are the meat, and the city is the pot; but I will remove you from it." The men used the pot picture to say they were safe. God uses the same picture and puts the slain in it, and the men are removed.

explanations.answer: The men standing at the gate
explanations.explanation: That's what the men said about themselves: "we are the meat." But God turns the picture around. In verse 7 the meat is "the slain you have laid within this city," and then He says, "but I will remove you from it." So the men don't end up in the pot.
The exiles aren't in this picture at all. Verse 7 puts the slain in the pot. The exiles show up later in the passage, when God speaks to Ezekiel about them in verses 14 and 15.

I can see why it sounds like a pot would keep them put. But God says the opposite in verse 7: "…but I will remove you from it." Then verse 9 adds, "I will bring you out of the city…" So they don't stay.
Right. In verse 7 God says, "…but I will remove you from it." The city was supposed to be their safe pot, but God says it won't be (verse 11). They're headed out.
Verse 8 says, "You fear the sword, so I will bring the sword against you, declares the Lord GOD." What they feared is what God says He will bring. Nobody's hiding in a pot from that.
Famine is a heavy word, but it isn't the one in verse 8. God says, "You fear the sword, so I will bring the sword against you." The sword is what they feared, so it's what God names.
No water anywhere in this verse, friend. Verse 8 says, "You fear the sword, so I will bring the sword against you." The sword is the answer.

That's the word. In verse 12 God says, "For you have neither followed My statutes nor practiced My ordinances, but you have conformed to the ordinances of the nations around you." God had given them His ordinances. They took the ones from the nations around them instead.
The priests aren't mentioned in this verse. God says they "have conformed to the ordinances of the nations around you." That's where they looked instead of at His statutes.
Nope, the prophets aren't in this verse. God says these men "have conformed to the ordinances of the nations around you." The nations are the ones they copied.

Verse 13 says it simply: "Now as I was prophesying, Pelatiah son of Benaiah died." He's one of the two leaders named at the gate. This is a heavy moment, and the text doesn't say more about how or why, so I won't either.
No running in this verse, friend. It says, "Pelatiah son of Benaiah died." He's one of the two leaders named at the gate, and this is a heavy moment.

The text doesn't say anything about Pelatiah repenting. Verse 13 says Pelatiah son of Benaiah, one of the two leaders named at the gate, died while Ezekiel was prophesying. It's a sobering line, and I'll leave it as the text has it.

explanations.answer: Will You bring the remnant of Israel to a complete end
explanations.explanation: Yes. Ezekiel falls facedown and cries, "Oh, Lord GOD, will You bring the remnant of Israel to a complete end?" I think this is a prayer from a man who just watched something hard happen right in front of him. The next thing in the text is the word of the LORD coming to him.

explanations.answer: Will You bring Pelatiah back to life again
explanations.explanation: That's a human thing to ask, but it isn't what Ezekiel says. In verse 13 he cries out, "Oh, Lord GOD, will You bring the remnant of Israel to a complete end?" His question is about the whole remnant of Israel.

explanations.answer: Will You send me home to the exiles now
explanations.explanation: Ezekiel doesn't ask for a ride home. Verse 13 has him falling facedown and crying out, "Oh, Lord GOD, will You bring the remnant of Israel to a complete end?" He's asking about the remnant, not about himself.

explanations.answer: They are far away from the LORD
explanations.explanation: That's what they say in verse 15: "They are far away from the LORD…" The people of Jerusalem were talking about Ezekiel's brothers, his relatives and fellow exiles. God repeats what was said, so He heard every word of it.

explanations.answer: They will be coming home soon
explanations.explanation: That's a friendlier thing than what was said. In verse 15 the people of Jerusalem say, "They are far away from the LORD…" There's nothing hopeful about it.

explanations.answer: They are the true leaders now
explanations.explanation: Nobody in Jerusalem was handing out titles to the exiles. Verse 15 says the people of Jerusalem said, "They are far away from the LORD…" That's the whole opinion.

That's what verse 15 says: "…this land has been given to us as a possession." The people of Jerusalem said it about themselves, right after saying the exiles were far from the LORD. God tells Ezekiel what they said, and then He answers it.
The text says they did. In verse 15, the people of Jerusalem say, "…this land has been given to us as a possession." It's the second half of what they were saying about the exiles.

God says, "…yet for a little while I have been a sanctuary for them in the countries to which they have gone." A sanctuary is a place of safety and nearness. The people in Jerusalem said the exiles were far from the LORD, and God's answer is that He has been a sanctuary for them even there.

That would match what the people of Jerusalem were saying. But God's answer in verse 16 is different: "…yet for a little while I have been a sanctuary for them in the countries to which they have gone." He isn't a stranger to them.
I get why you'd think so, with all the warnings earlier in the passage. But in verse 16 God says, "…for a little while I have been a sanctuary for them…" To these exiles, He says He's a sanctuary.

Verse 17 says, "I will gather you from the peoples and assemble you from the countries to which you have been scattered, and I will give back to you the land of Israel." The people of Jerusalem said the land was theirs. God says He'll give it back to the exiles.
A throne would be a big promise, but it isn't in this verse. God says, "…I will give back to you the land of Israel." The promise is the land.
No crown in this promise, friend. In verse 17 God says, "…I will give back to you the land of Israel." Land is what He gives back.
It's the other way around. Verse 18 says, "When they return to it, they will remove all its detestable things and all its abominations." They don't leave those things behind. They clear them out.

Right. God says in verse 18, "When they return to it, they will remove all its detestable things and all its abominations." The exiles come back and clear the place out. Nothing detestable gets left on the shelf.
Yes. God says, "I will remove their heart of stone and give them a heart of flesh…" (Ezekiel 11:19). Stone doesn't bend, and God takes it out. This is the promise God makes about the exiles' hearts.
Fire sounds dramatic, but it isn't in the verse. God says, "I will remove their heart of stone and give them a heart of flesh…" Stone is what comes out.
Wax isn't in this verse, and I think it's easy to guess it, since it sounds like something soft. God says, "I will remove their heart of stone…" Stone is the one that comes out.
That's the one. God says, "I will remove their heart of stone and give them a heart of flesh…" A heart of flesh is the opposite of stone. It's a heart God gives, not one they make.
Bronze is strong, but this promise isn't about strong. God says, "I will remove their heart of stone and give them a heart of flesh…" Flesh is what He puts in.
Glass doesn't show up in this verse. After taking out the heart of stone, God says, "…and give them a heart of flesh…" Flesh is the word.

explanations.answer: So they may follow His statutes
explanations.explanation: Verse 20 says, "…so that they may follow My statutes, keep My ordinances, and practice them." Earlier, God said the men at the gate hadn't followed His statutes. Here He gives the exiles a new heart and a new spirit so that they can.

explanations.answer: So they may rebuild the walls
explanations.explanation: Walls aren't mentioned anywhere in this promise. Verse 20 says God gives the new heart "so that they may follow My statutes, keep My ordinances, and practice them." That's the reason the text gives.

explanations.answer: So they may rule the nations
explanations.explanation: That's a big job, but it isn't in this verse. God says in verse 20 that He gives the new heart "so that they may follow My statutes, keep My ordinances, and practice them." Following His ways is the reason.

That's right, word for word from verse 20: "Then they will be My people, and I will be their God." It comes right after the new heart and the following of His statutes. This is the promise God makes to the exiles.
The words are in the text. Verse 20 says, "Then they will be My people, and I will be their God." God says this to the exiles.

Verse 23 says, "And the glory of the LORD rose up from within the city and stood over the mountain east of the city." The glory had been at the east gate earlier in the vision. Now it rises from within the city and stands over the mountain to the east.
West is the opposite way. Verse 23 says the glory of the LORD "stood over the mountain east of the city." East is the direction.
North isn't the direction in the text. Verse 23 says the glory of the LORD rose up from within the city and "stood over the mountain east of the city." It's east, friend.

explanations.answer: He tells them everything the LORD showed him
explanations.explanation: Yes. Verse 25 says, "I told the exiles everything the LORD had shown me." He doesn't hold a single piece back. A vision like this, the gate, the pot, the new heart and the glory rising, goes straight to the exiles.

explanations.answer: He keeps every part of it to himself
explanations.explanation: It's the other way around. Ezekiel says, "I told the exiles everything the LORD had shown me." Nothing stays locked up inside him.

explanations.answer: He shares it only with the other priests
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't narrow it to one group. Verse 25 says Ezekiel "told the exiles everything the LORD had shown me." The exiles are the ones who hear it, and they hear all of it.
